topics.title: Humidity measures (dew point, RH, mixing ratio)
lesson: Several quantities describe how much water vapour is in the air. Knowing which ones change with temperature and which do not is a favourite exam question.

list: Vapour pressure (e): the part of total pressure due to water vapour.
Saturation vapour pressure (es): the maximum vapour pressure possible at a given temperature. It rises quickly with temperature, roughly 7% per 1 C.
Relative humidity (RH) = e / es x 100%. It depends on temperature, so it changes when air is warmed or cooled even if no moisture is added.
Dew point (Td): temperature at which the air would be saturated. It measures the actual moisture content and is not affected by simple warming or cooling.
Mixing ratio (w) and specific humidity (q): mass of vapour per mass of dry air (or of total air), in g/kg. Conserved in an unsaturated rising or sinking parcel.
Wet-bulb temperature (Tw): lowest temperature reachable by evaporating water into the air. Always between the dew point and air temperature.

lesson.formula: Td <= Tw <= T     (all equal when RH = 100%)

lesson: A sling or aspirated psychrometer reads dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures, from which dew point and RH are found.
Below 0 C the frost point (saturation with respect to ice) is slightly higher than the dew point. This matters for frost and rime formation.

lesson.note: Remember: dew point tells you how much moisture there is. RH tells you how close you are to saturation.

terms: Mass of water vapour per unit mass of dry air, usually g/kg.
Temperature a parcel reaches when cooled to saturation by evaporation.
Maximum vapour pressure at a given temperature.

questions.q: Which humidity measure stays constant as an unsaturated parcel rises?
questions.e: Mixing ratio is a mass ratio and is conserved if no vapour is added or removed. RH, vapour pressure and dew point all change with pressure or temperature.

questions.q: What is the correct ordering of temperature, wet-bulb and dew point for unsaturated air?
questions.e: Air temperature is highest, dew point lowest, wet-bulb in between. They are equal only at saturation.

questions.q: How does saturation vapour pressure change with temperature?
questions.e: Warmer air can hold much more water vapour; the relationship is roughly exponential.

questions.q: What is true when relative humidity is 100%?
questions.e: Saturation means the air temperature has reached the dew point.

questions.q: A room is heated with no moisture added. What happens to the dew point and RH?
c: Dew point stays the same, RH falls
questions.e: Dew point reflects moisture content (unchanged). Warmer air has a higher es, so RH drops.

questions.q: The dry-bulb temperature is 12 C and the wet-bulb is 8 C. Where is the dew point most likely?
questions.e: For unsaturated air Td < Tw < T.

questions.q: What are the usual units of mixing ratio?
c: Grams of vapour per kilogram of dry air
Hectopascals of vapour pressure per kilometre of height
Percent of the saturation value at the same temperature
Degrees Celsius of dew point depression for each metre
questions.e: Mixing ratio is the mass of vapour per mass of dry air, typically g/kg.

questions.q: Air is warmed at constant pressure with no moisture added. What happens to the vapour pressure?
questions.e: Vapour pressure depends on moisture content, not on temperature.

questions.q: Saturated air is cooled further. What happens?
c: The dew point rises above the temperature
questions.e: Cooling saturated air removes capacity, so the excess vapour condenses.

questions.q: Which instrument gives dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures?
questions.e: A psychrometer has two thermometers, one with a wetted wick.

questions.q: Below 0 C, how does the frost point compare with the dew point?
questions.e: Saturation over ice occurs at a slightly higher temperature than over supercooled water.

topics.title: Condensation, saturation and lifting mechanisms
lesson: Cloud forms when air becomes saturated and water vapour condenses onto tiny particles.

list: Cooling is the usual route: adiabatic cooling by lifting (most important), radiational cooling at night, advection over a cold surface, mixing of two nearly saturated air masses.
Adding moisture: evaporation from rain falling into dry air, air moving over warm water or wet ground.

lesson: Pure vapour does not condense easily. Cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) such as sea salt, dust and smoke provide surfaces. Salt-rich maritime air has plenty, which is why sea fog forms readily on the coast.
Cloud droplets can stay liquid well below 0 C. Supercooled water is common between 0 C and about -20 C and may persist to about -40 C. This is the root of aircraft icing.

list: Convection: surface heating produces thermals and cumulus.
Orographic: air forced up terrain.
Frontal: warm air rising over or being pushed up by cold air.
Convergence: horizontal inflow forces air upward, for example around a low or along a sea breeze front.

lesson.note: Subsidence (sinking air) is not a lifting mechanism. It warms the air, lowers RH, and dissipates cloud.

terms: Cloud condensation nuclei: tiny particles on which droplets form.
Liquid water at temperatures below 0 C.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a lifting mechanism?
questions.e: Subsidence is sinking motion, which warms and dries the air.

questions.q: What role do condensation nuclei play?
c: They give water vapour surfaces on which to condense
They warm the air so that its saturation point is lowered
They absorb moisture from the cloud and so remove it from the air
They lower the pressure inside droplets so that droplets evaporate
questions.e: Particles such as salt and dust allow droplets to form at or near saturation.

questions.q: What is the most important way air is cooled to saturation in cloud formation?
questions.e: Lifting leads to expansion and cooling, producing most clouds and precipitation.

questions.q: Can liquid cloud droplets exist at temperatures below 0 C?
c: Yes, supercooled droplets can persist to about -40 C
No, cloud droplets always freeze the moment they pass 0 C
Yes, but only within a degree or two of the freezing point
No, liquid water can exist only above 0 C at any height
questions.e: Supercooled water is common in clouds and is the source of aircraft icing.

questions.q: Convergence as a lifting mechanism occurs when:
questions.e: Converging air has nowhere to go but up.

questions.q: Orographic lifting is air forced to rise over:
c: Hills, mountains or other high terrain
A layer of colder air at a front
questions.e: Orographic means caused by terrain.

questions.q: Which of these cools air to saturation WITHOUT lifting?
c: Adiabatic expansion as the air rises over a hill or mountain
Frontal ascent over a wedge of colder air near the surface
Orographic ascent along the windward slope of a mountain range
questions.e: Radiation removes heat from the surface layer without any vertical motion.

questions.q: Why are sea salt particles important in cloud formation?
c: They act as cloud condensation nuclei
They prevent condensation by keeping the air supersaturated
They absorb sunlight and warm the surrounding cloud layer
They cool the sea surface and lower the dew point of the air
questions.e: Salt particles are hygroscopic and attract water vapour.

questions.q: Convergence of surface winds typically leads to:
questions.e: Mass that flows in must rise.

questions.q: Which lifting mechanism comes from daytime heating of the ground?
questions.e: Heated ground warms the air above it, which rises as thermals.

questions.q: Why can mixing two nearly saturated air masses produce cloud?
c: The saturation curve is non-linear, so the mixture can exceed saturation
Mixing always releases latent heat and warms the mixture past saturation
Mixing lowers the pressure of both parcels below the saturation value
Mixing removes condensation nuclei so drops grow faster by collision
questions.e: Because saturation vapour pressure is a curve, the mix can be supersaturated.

topics.title: Cloud classification and genera
lesson: Clouds are classified by form (stratiform, cumuliform, cirriform) and by height of the base. Ten basic types (genera) cover all clouds. Heights below are approximate for mid-latitudes; check the exact definitions in your course material.

lesson.h: High (about 5 to 13 km, above 18,000 to 20,000 ft)

list: Cirrus (Ci): thin, wispy, ice crystals.
Cirrocumulus (Cc): small white ripples or grains.
Cirrostratus (Cs): thin veil. Produces a halo around the sun or moon. Often the first sign of an approaching warm front.
Altocumulus (Ac): patchy layers or globules.
Altostratus (As): grey sheet through which the sun appears as a dim disc. No halo. Precipitation may follow.
Stratus (St): uniform grey layer, drizzle possible. Fog that has lifted.
Stratocumulus (Sc): lumpy layer, common over the Atlantic.
Nimbostratus (Ns): thick, dark layer with steady rain or snow, often extends into middle levels.
Cumulus (Cu): heaped, flat base, fair weather to towering.
Cumulonimbus (Cb): very deep convective cloud from low levels to the tropopause. Thunderstorms, hail, anvil top.

lesson.note: Cirrus to cirrostratus to altostratus to nimbostratus is the classic sequence ahead of a warm front.

terms: Flat spreading top of a cumulonimbus, usually of ice crystals.

questions.q: Which cloud is associated with thunderstorms, hail and a spreading anvil?
questions.e: Cumulonimbus is the deep convective cloud that produces thunderstorms.

questions.q: A halo around the sun is a sign of which cloud?
questions.e: Ice crystals in cirrostratus refract light to form halos.

questions.q: Which cloud produces steady, widespread rain or snow from a thick grey layer?
questions.e: Nimbostratus is a thick layer cloud associated with continuous precipitation.

questions.q: What is the typical cloud sequence ahead of an approaching warm front?
questions.e: Cloud thickens and lowers as the warm front nears: Ci, Cs, As, Ns.

questions.q: A grey layer cloud lets the sun appear as a dim, watery disc without a halo. What cloud is it?
questions.e: Altostratus is thick enough to dim the sun but not to hide it completely, and it lacks the halo of cirrostratus.

questions.q: Which of these clouds is made mostly of ice crystals?
questions.e: Cirrus forms at very cold levels, where cloud is made of ice.

questions.q: What is cumulus congestus?
c: A towering cumulus that can grow into cumulonimbus
A thin, high cloud made of ice crystals that produces halos
A layer of low stratus formed by cooling in light winds
A lens-shaped cloud that forms in the crest of a mountain wave
questions.e: Congestus is a vigorous growing cumulus with great vertical depth.

questions.q: Which cloud commonly produces drizzle?
questions.e: Stratus is a low, uniform layer of fine droplets.

questions.q: Altostratus belongs to which level?
c: It is not classified by level
questions.e: The 'alto' prefix means middle level.

questions.q: Which cloud has a smooth lens shape and marks mountain waves?
questions.e: Lenticular clouds form at the crests of stationary waves.

questions.q: Which cloud type is common over cold Atlantic water in a moist, stable onshore flow?
c: Cumulonimbus, because the cold sea heats the air above it
Cirrus only, because the stable air stops all low cloud forming
Altocumulus lenticularis, since the sea acts like a mountain range
questions.e: Stable moist flow over cool water produces low layer cloud.

topics.title: Precipitation processes (warm rain, ice crystal)
lesson: Cloud droplets (about 0.01 mm) are far too small to fall. Precipitation needs droplets to grow a million times in volume by one of two processes.

In clouds warmer than 0 C, larger droplets fall faster, collide with smaller ones, and merge. Needs a deep cloud with strong updraft and lots of liquid water. Dominant in the tropics and in warm maritime clouds.

In mixed clouds containing supercooled water and ice, the saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over water. Vapour therefore moves from droplets to ice crystals, which grow quickly and fall. Most mid-latitude rain starts as snow that melts on the way down.

list: Rain, drizzle (drops smaller than 0.5 mm), snow, graupel (rimed snow pellets).
Hail: layered ice from strong cumulonimbus updrafts.
Ice pellets (sleet): raindrops refreeze in a deep cold layer near the surface.
Freezing rain: supercooled raindrops freeze on contact. It needs a warm layer aloft and a shallow below-freezing layer at the ground. Very hazardous.

lesson.note: Ice pellets mean a deep cold layer. Freezing rain means a shallow one. Both come from the same warm-layer-aloft setup.

terms: Growth of ice crystals at the expense of supercooled droplets.
Soft pellets formed by supercooled droplets freezing onto snow crystals.

questions.q: Why does the Bergeron process work?
c: Saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over liquid water
Saturation vapour pressure over ice is higher than over liquid water
Ice crystals are heavier than droplets so they collide with them more often
Supercooled droplets freeze solid as soon as they touch any ice crystal
questions.e: At the same temperature, air saturated with respect to water is supersaturated with respect to ice, so crystals grow while droplets evaporate.

questions.q: Which process dominates precipitation formation in warm tropical clouds?
questions.e: Warm clouds lack ice, so droplets grow by colliding and merging.

questions.q: Freezing rain most commonly forms when:
c: Snow melts in a warm layer aloft and falls into a shallow sub-freezing layer at the ground
Rain falls through a deep layer of sub-freezing air and refreezes completely before landing
Hail melts in the warm air near the ground and refreezes on cold surfaces below
Strong updrafts carry raindrops above the freezing level and drop them as clear ice
questions.e: Drops are liquid when they reach the cold surface layer too briefly to refreeze, then freeze on contact.

questions.q: What distinguishes ice pellets from freezing rain?
c: Ice pellets form where the cold layer near the surface is deep enough to refreeze drops before landing
Ice pellets form only in thunderstorms with strong updrafts, while freezing rain forms in layer cloud
Ice pellets are raindrops that freeze on contact with the ground, unlike freezing rain, which freezes in the air
Ice pellets form when the surface temperature is above 0 C and the whole column is above freezing
questions.e: In a deeper sub-freezing layer, raindrops refreeze in the air and arrive as ice pellets.

questions.q: Which precipitation type is associated with strong updrafts in cumulonimbus?
questions.e: Strong updrafts keep stones aloft where they accumulate layers of ice.

questions.q: Drizzle drops have a diameter smaller than about:
questions.e: Drizzle drops are under about 0.5 mm; larger drops are rain.

questions.q: What does hail growth require?
c: Strong updrafts holding stones in supercooled water
Calm, stable air with a deep layer of warm, moist cloud
Warm clouds only, with no ice and no supercooled water
A fog layer at the ground with very light surface winds
questions.e: Updrafts recycle stones through supercooled water so layers of ice build up.

questions.q: In the Bergeron process, which grow at the expense of which?
c: Ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets
Droplets grow at the expense of ice crystals in mixed cloud
Hailstones grow at the expense of the surrounding rain drops
Fog droplets grow at the expense of the cloud base layer
questions.e: Vapour moves from droplets to the lower-pressure environment over ice.

questions.q: What is graupel?
c: A soft ice pellet formed by riming of snow crystals
A frozen raindrop with a clear, solid ice structure
A large hailstone that has fallen from a cumulonimbus anvil
A frost deposit that forms on cold surfaces on clear nights
questions.e: Supercooled droplets freeze onto a snow crystal and build a pellet.

questions.q: Which precipitation falls as liquid but freezes on contact with the surface?
questions.e: Freezing rain is supercooled liquid that freezes when it hits a cold surface.

questions.q: A deep warm layer aloft above a deep cold layer near the ground typically gives:
questions.e: A deep cold layer refreezes the drops before they land.

topics.title: Fog types and formation
lesson: Fog is cloud at ground level. It is reported when visibility is below 1 km (5/8 statute mile). Mist (BR) is a less dense obstruction.

list: Radiation fog: clear skies, light winds, moist air, long nights. The ground cools by radiation and chills the air above to the dew point. Forms at night in valleys, burns off after sunrise. Common inland in fall.

Advection fog: warm moist air moves over a colder surface and is cooled to saturation. Sea fog is the classic case. Over Nova Scotia's south shore and the Grand Banks it is frequent in spring and summer, when warm southerly flow crosses cold ocean water. Can persist day and night.
Upslope fog: moist air forced up rising terrain cools adiabatically.
Steam fog (sea smoke): very cold air over warm water. Water evaporates into the air and condenses immediately. Seen over lakes and the ocean in winter.
Precipitation (frontal) fog: rain falling into cooler air evaporates, saturating the layer near the surface. Common ahead of warm fronts.
Small temperature-dew point spread and falling temperature.
Light wind (about 2 to 7 kt) favours radiation fog. Strong wind lifts it into stratus.
Advection fog requires a warm moist flow over a cold surface.

lesson.note: Wind speed is the main separator: calm to light for radiation fog, moderate onshore flow for sea fog.

terms: Greatest distance at which objects can be seen and recognized.
Horizontal transport of air properties by wind.

questions.q: Which conditions favour radiation fog?
c: Clear skies, light winds, moist air, long nights
Overcast skies, strong winds, dry air, short days
Warm moist air flowing over a much colder surface at speed
Cold dry air moving over relatively warm open water
questions.e: Clear skies allow strong radiational cooling; light wind prevents mixing from lifting the fog layer.

questions.q: Fog along Nova Scotia's south shore in summer is typically:
questions.e: Warm moist southerly flow over cold coastal water cools to saturation.

questions.q: How does steam fog form?
c: Cold air passes over relatively warm water
Warm air passes over cold water
Air is lifted up a slope
questions.e: Evaporation from the warm water saturates the cold air immediately above it.

questions.q: What is the reporting threshold for fog?
questions.e: Fog is reported when visibility drops below 1 km; mist is between 5/8 SM and 6 SM in Canadian reports.

questions.q: Rain evaporating into cool air below a warm front can produce:
questions.e: Rain adds moisture to the air near the surface, which can saturate and form fog.

questions.q: When does radiation fog normally dissipate?
c: Shortly after sunrise as heating warms the surface layer
As the sun sets and the surface begins to cool again
When the wind drops to calm and the sky stays clear all day
When the dew point rises 5 C above the air temperature
questions.e: Solar heating warms the air and evaporates the fog.

questions.q: Mist is reported when visibility is:
questions.e: In Canadian reports BR is used for visibility from 5/8 SM to 6 SM.

questions.q: Winds above about 15 kt tend to convert radiation fog into:
questions.e: Stronger mixing lifts the fog layer into stratus.

questions.q: Fog is most likely when the temperature-dew point spread is:
questions.e: A very small spread means the air is nearly saturated.

questions.q: Why can advection fog persist in strong onshore winds?
c: Warm moist air keeps flowing over cold water
questions.e: As long as the air keeps crossing a cold surface it keeps cooling.

questions.q: Sea smoke occurs most often:
c: In winter, when very cold air flows over open water
On calm summer nights when the sea is cooler than the air
When warm, moist air crosses a cold sea surface in spring
Over dry desert areas in the afternoon after strong heating
questions.e: It needs a large temperature difference with colder air above warmer water.

topics.title: Icing and its causes
lesson: Aircraft icing happens when supercooled liquid drops hit an airframe below 0 C and freeze on contact. It increases weight and drag, reduces lift, and can block pitot tubes and engine inlets.

list: Rime ice: small droplets freeze instantly, trapping air. Opaque, white, rough and brittle. Common in stratiform cloud at temperatures of about -10 to -20 C.
Clear ice: large drops spread before freezing. Smooth, hard, transparent and heavy. Found at 0 to about -10 C, in cumuliform cloud, and in freezing rain. More dangerous.
Mixed ice: combination of both.
Freezing rain and freezing drizzle: severe, and usually the strongest icing threat.
Cumuliform clouds with strong updrafts and large water content.
Frontal zones where warm moist air rises over cold air.
Carburettor icing: can occur at outside temperatures well above freezing (up to about 20 C or higher) with high humidity, because vaporization and pressure drop cool the carburettor.
Frost on the ground: forms by deposition when the surface is below 0 C. Must be removed before takeoff.

lesson.note: Anti-icing and de-icing equipment may not handle severe icing. If in doubt, avoid. A change of altitude to warmer air or out of cloud is the standard escape.

terms: Opaque, rough ice formed by small droplets freezing on impact.
Smooth, transparent, heavy ice formed by large drops.
Ice that forms in a carburettor due to cooling from fuel vaporization and pressure drop.

questions.q: What causes clear ice?
c: Large supercooled drops that spread and freeze slowly
Tiny supercooled droplets that freeze instantly on impact
Frost deposited on a cold airframe on the ground at night
Hailstones striking and sticking to the leading edges
questions.e: Large drops flow back along the surface before freezing, forming a smooth, dense layer.

questions.q: Which condition normally poses the greatest structural icing threat?
questions.e: Freezing rain has large supercooled drops and a high water content.

questions.q: Carburettor icing can occur:
c: At temperatures well above freezing in humid air
Only when outside air is below -10 C in dry air
Only in visible moisture such as freezing rain at 0 C or lower
Only on the ground before engine start in heavy snow
questions.e: Cooling in the carburettor can drop temperature below 0 C even when the outside air is as warm as 20 C.

questions.q: How does rime ice look?
questions.e: Small drops freeze quickly and trap air bubbles, giving a milky appearance.

questions.q: What is a standard escape from structural icing?
c: Change altitude to warmer air or leave the cloud
Climb higher where the air is colder and drier
Increase airspeed and stay in the same layer until clear
Turn off the anti-ice system to save engine power
questions.e: Moving out of the supercooled water zone, usually to warmer or clear air, stops further accumulation.

questions.q: In which temperature range is supercooled water most commonly found in clouds?
questions.e: Supercooled water is most common between 0 and about -20 C.

questions.q: What effect does ice on the wing leading edge have?
c: There is no effect on lift
questions.e: Ice disturbs the airflow, reduces lift and increases weight and drag.

questions.q: Severe icing means:
c: Accumulation is so fast that de-icing equipment cannot control it
Ice is visible on the aircraft but does not affect performance
Ice forms only on the ground and never builds up in flight
Ice forms only in clear air and has no effect on the engine
questions.e: In severe icing an immediate diversion is required.

questions.q: Frost on the wings before takeoff must be:
c: Ignored since it does not change airflow
Left alone because it blows off during the takeoff roll
questions.e: Even thin frost can spoil lift, so it must be removed.

questions.q: Which cloud typically has the highest liquid water content and large drops?
c: Cirrus, because high ice crystal clouds hold the most water
Cirrostratus, because it covers a large area of the sky
Thin altostratus, because it forms in a stable layer aloft
questions.e: Strong updrafts carry plenty of liquid water above the freezing level.

questions.q: Where is structural icing least likely?
c: In cloud-free air at temperatures below -40 C
In freezing rain at the surface at temperatures just below zero
In supercooled towering cumulus at about -10 C
In stratocumulus at -8 C with a high liquid water content
questions.e: Without liquid water there is nothing to freeze on the aircraft.
